subtopic_detail: A midline neck lump in a school aged boy that rides upward when he puts his tongue out
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general outpatient clinic seeing a 6 year old boy whose mother noticed a lump in the front of his neck about six weeks ago. It has not changed in size and he has no pain, no difficulty swallowing and no hoarseness.

He is thriving on the 60th centile for weight and height and has had no recent sore throat or febrile illness. On examination there is a smooth 2 cm swelling in the midline just above the thyroid cartilage. It is not tender and the overlying skin is normal. When you ask him to protrude his tongue, the lump moves upward; it does not move when he swallows a sip of water.

data_table.Examination: Smooth non-tender 2 cm midline swelling above the thyroid cartilage, rises on tongue protrusion, no movement on swallowing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, thyroid gland not separately palpable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his assessment?

options.text: Ultrasound of the neck with thyroid function tests
options.rationale: A midline swelling that elevates on tongue protrusion sits along the embryological tract of the thyroglossal duct, and ultrasound both confirms the cystic lesion and documents that a normally sited thyroid gland is present before any excision. Thyroid function is checked because the cyst occasionally contains the only functioning thyroid tissue the child has. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

options.text: Fine needle aspiration of the lump in clinic today
options.rationale: Aspiration of a cystic midline lesion risks introducing infection into a tract that will later need surgical excision, and it does not answer the question the surgeon needs answered, which is whether functioning thyroid tissue lies elsewhere. Cytology would be the right first move for a suspicious solid lateral nodal mass, which this is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

options.text: Contrast computed tomography of the neck and chest
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging with ionising radiation is not required for a clinically typical midline cyst and would be reserved for a mass with features suggesting malignancy or airway compromise. Ultrasound answers the anatomical question in a child without a radiation dose. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

options.text: A ten day course of oral amoxicillin and review
options.rationale: There is no erythema, tenderness or fever to suggest infection, so antibiotics treat nothing and delay definitive assessment. Antibiotics would be appropriate if the cyst had become acutely infected, in which case excision is deferred until the inflammation settles. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Excision of the lump on the next elective list
options.rationale: Excision is the eventual treatment but proceeding before imaging risks removing a child's only thyroid tissue and leaving them permanently hypothyroid without anticipating it. The near pair here is that the operation itself is correct while the sequencing is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck lumps)

explanation.summary: Paediatric neck lumps divide usefully by position, with midline lesions dominated by thyroglossal remnants and dermoid cysts and lateral lesions by reactive nodes and branchial remnants. The thyroglossal duct runs from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to the final position of the thyroid gland, which is why traction on a remnant cyst causes it to rise when the tongue is protruded. Definitive treatment is the Sistrunk procedure, in which the central portion of the hyoid bone is removed along with the tract, because simple cyst excision leaves tract epithelium behind and recurrence follows. Imaging before surgery matters because a small proportion of these cysts contain ectopic tissue that represents the child's entire functioning thyroid.
key_points: Elevation on tongue protrusion localises the lesion to the thyroglossal tract
Ultrasound confirms a normally sited thyroid gland before excision
Definitive surgery removes the central hyoid with the tract, not the cyst alone
Acute infection defers surgery until inflammation has settled
Dermoid cysts are also midline but do not move with the tongue
explanation.pearls: Simple cyst excision without removing the central third of the hyoid bone carries a recurrence rate of around 40 to 50 per cent, which falls below 5 per cent with the Sistrunk procedure, so the operation named in the referral matters as much as the decision to operate.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of neck lumps in children

subtopic_detail: A two month old who holds her head tilted to one side with a firm swelling within one neck muscle and full passive range achievable
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing an 8 week old girl whose parents say she always holds her head tipped towards her right shoulder and prefers to look to the left. She was born at term by vacuum extraction after a prolonged second stage.

She feeds well and smiles responsively. On examination her head is tilted to the right with her chin rotated to the left. There is a firm painless fusiform swelling within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. You can passively rotate her chin fully to the right and tilt her left ear to her left shoulder, although she resists the last few degrees. Her red reflexes are present and symmetrical and she fixes and follows across the midline in both directions.

data_table.Examination: Head tilted right with chin rotated left, firm fusiform 1.5 cm swelling within the right sternocleidomastoid, full passive cervical rotation and lateral flexion achievable with resistance at end range, occiput symmetrical with no flattening, red reflexes present bilaterally, fixes and follows across the midline, tone and reflexes normal in all four limbs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for cranial orthotic helmet fitting this month
options.rationale: A helmet treats established skull deformity, and her occiput is symmetrical with no flattening, so there is nothing for an orthosis to remodel. Positional skull flattening is a common secondary consequence of untreated head tilt, which is an argument for starting physiotherapy now rather than for fitting a helmet. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for positioning and stretching
options.rationale: A fusiform swelling within the sternocleidomastoid in an infant with a traumatic delivery and a passively correctable tilt is the typical picture, and supervised stretching with positioning advice resolves the great majority when started in the first few months. Earlier referral predicts both faster resolution and a lower chance of needing surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange ultrasound of both sternocleidomastoid muscles
options.rationale: Imaging the muscle adds nothing when the mass is palpable within it and the neck corrects passively, and it delays the treatment that actually changes the outcome. Ultrasound of the neck earns its place when a mass lies outside the muscle or the tilt does not correct, raising the possibility of another lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to ophthalmology for assessment of eye movements
options.rationale: Ocular torticollis from a fourth nerve palsy or nystagmus produces a compensatory head posture without a muscle mass, and here she fixes and follows across the midline in both directions with symmetrical red reflexes. That combination makes an ocular cause very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange cervical spine radiographs before any treatment
options.rationale: Radiographs look for vertebral anomalies such as hemivertebrae or atlantoaxial abnormality, which present with a fixed tilt that will not correct passively. Full passive correction with a palpable muscle mass points away from a bony cause. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis is the commonest cause of a fixed head tilt in early infancy and is associated with instrumental or difficult delivery, breech presentation and intrauterine crowding. The diagnosis is clinical and rests on a tilt towards the affected muscle with chin rotation away from it, often with a palpable pseudotumour within the muscle belly in the first weeks. The important differentials are ocular torticollis, vertebral anomaly, posterior fossa or spinal cord lesions, and in older children an acquired cause such as an atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation or a retropharyngeal abscess; each produces a tilt that does not correct passively or is accompanied by neurological or systemic signs. Untreated tilt drives positional skull flattening and facial asymmetry, and hip examination matters because developmental dysplasia of the hip is more common in these infants.
key_points: Tilt towards the affected muscle with chin rotation away from it is the pattern
A palpable mass within the muscle belly supports the diagnosis and settles over months
Passive correctability is the feature that separates muscular from bony causes
Physiotherapy started in the first months resolves the large majority
Screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip in the same consultation
explanation.pearls: Referral before 3 months of age is associated with resolution in over 90 per cent with stretching alone, while referral after 12 months raises the likelihood of needing surgical release substantially, so the age at referral is the single strongest modifiable predictor of outcome.

subtopic_detail: A toddler who will not use one arm after being lifted by the hand, holding it slightly bent with the palm turned down
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 2 year old girl brought in by her father an hour after she refused to use her left arm. He had been holding her hand as she stepped off a kerb, she stumbled, and he pulled her up by the hand to stop her falling. She cried briefly and has not used the arm since.

She is playing happily with her right hand and is not distressed at rest. She holds the left arm slightly flexed at the elbow with the forearm turned palm down and resists any attempt to turn the palm up. There is no swelling, deformity or bruising anywhere along the arm, and palpation of the clavicle, humerus, elbow, forearm and wrist produces no localised tenderness.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held in slight elbow flexion and forearm pronation, active supination refused, no swelling deformity or bruising, no focal bony tenderness over clavicle humerus elbow forearm or wrist, radial pulse present with normal capillary refill and warm hand

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange radiographs of the elbow before any manipulation
options.rationale: Radiographs are normal in this condition and are reserved for an atypical mechanism, focal bony tenderness, swelling or deformity, or failure of a reduction attempt. Imaging every child with this classic history delays a bedside manoeuvre that works within minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling and review in the fracture clinic
options.rationale: Immobilisation leaves the annular ligament entrapped and the child not using the arm for days when a single manoeuvre restores function immediately. A sling with clinic review is the right answer for an undisplaced fracture, which the absence of focal tenderness makes unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Reduce it by supination and flexion of the affected elbow
options.rationale: Axial traction on a pronated forearm slips the annular ligament over the radial head, and supinating the forearm then flexing the elbow fully reduces it, usually with a palpable click and return of use within 5 to 30 minutes. A hyperpronation manoeuvre is an equally accepted alternative with comparable success. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for reduction under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: This is a bedside procedure that needs no anaesthesia and no specialist involvement when the history and examination are typical. Orthopaedic referral becomes appropriate only after two or three failed attempts or if imaging shows a fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Arrange ultrasound of the elbow to look for an effusion
options.rationale: Ultrasound is not part of the assessment pathway for this diagnosis and an effusion is neither expected nor relevant to treatment. Looking for a joint effusion with ultrasound belongs to the assessment of an irritable hip or a suspected septic joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation, usually called pulled elbow, accounts for a large share of upper limb presentations in children between 1 and 4 years and follows longitudinal traction on an extended pronated arm. The annular ligament is relatively lax at this age and slips proximally over the radial head, and it tightens again once the radius is reduced, which is why recurrence becomes uncommon after about age 5. The key clinical discriminator is the combination of a pronated resting posture with refusal to supinate and the complete absence of swelling, deformity or focal bony tenderness. Where the history is not witnessed or does not fit, a supracondylar or forearm fracture and inflicted injury both need active consideration before any manipulation.
key_points: Typical age is 1 to 4 years with traction on a pronated extended arm
Pronated posture with refused supination and no focal tenderness is the pattern
Radiographs are normal and reserved for atypical cases or failed reduction
Supination with flexion or hyperpronation both reduce it at the bedside
Recurrence is common under age 5 and parents need anticipatory advice
explanation.pearls: After a successful manoeuvre most children use the arm again within 5 to 30 minutes, so a deliberate period of observation with a toy offered at shoulder height is the confirmatory test; persistent non-use beyond 30 minutes after two attempts is the trigger for radiographs.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

subtopic_detail: A four month old whose eye waters and crusts every morning since the first weeks of life with a clear white eye between episodes
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4 month old boy whose mother says his left eye has been watery since he was about two weeks old and that it is gummed shut with yellow crust most mornings. She wipes it clean and the eye looks normal for the rest of the day. He has had three courses of eye drops from different doctors with no lasting change.

He is thriving, immunised on schedule and otherwise well. On examination the left eye is watery with a tear film that overflows onto the cheek. The conjunctiva is white with no injection and the cornea is clear. Gentle pressure over the medial canthus produces a small bead of mucoid material at the inner corner. Red reflexes are present and symmetrical and the corneal diameters look equal.

data_table.Examination: Left eye with overflowing tear film and dried crust on the lashes, white non-injected conjunctiva, clear cornea, mucoid reflux from the medial canthus on pressure over the lacrimal sac, red reflexes present and symmetrical, corneal diameters equal with no photophobia or blepharospasm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer for probing of the tear duct under anaesthesia now
options.rationale: Probing is reserved for obstruction that persists beyond about 12 months of age, because the great majority canalise spontaneously in the first year and early probing exposes an infant to anaesthesia for a self resolving condition. Earlier referral is warranted if there is a distended lacrimal sac or recurrent dacryocystitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Sticky eye)

options.text: Prescribe chloramphenicol 0.5 per cent eye drops for a week
options.rationale: Repeated topical antibiotics do not relieve a mechanical outflow obstruction and the white uninjected conjunctiva shows there is no conjunctivitis to treat, which is why three previous courses made no difference. Antibiotic drops are appropriate for a genuinely red eye with purulent discharge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently to ophthalmology for measurement of pressures
options.rationale: Infantile glaucoma causes watering but with photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and an enlarged corneal diameter, none of which is present here. Those features, or an asymmetric red reflex, would make urgent referral mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Sticky eye)

options.text: Advise lacrimal sac massage and review at twelve months
options.rationale: Mucoid reflux on pressure over the sac with a white eye localises the problem to a blocked nasolacrimal duct, and around 90 per cent open spontaneously during the first year, so cleaning with water and downward massage over the sac with review towards the end of the first year is the appropriate plan. Parents are advised to return sooner for a red or swollen sac or a genuinely inflamed eye. (Source: RCH CPG: Sticky eye)

options.text: Send a conjunctival swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea now
options.rationale: Those organisms cause a florid purulent conjunctivitis with marked lid swelling in the first weeks of life, not four months of intermittent morning crusting on a white eye. A swab is mandatory for purulent neonatal conjunctivitis in the first month. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction affects up to a fifth of infants and reflects failure of the distal duct to canalise at the valve of Hasner. The picture is watering and morning crusting from stagnant tears with a white conjunctiva, which distinguishes it from conjunctivitis, and mucoid reflux from the sac on digital pressure confirms it. The conditions that must not be missed are infantile glaucoma, signalled by photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding or enlargement, and dacryocystitis, signalled by a tender erythematous swelling over the sac needing systemic antibiotics. Spontaneous resolution occurs in the large majority within the first year, so referral for probing is timed to persistence beyond about 12 months rather than to parental frustration.
key_points: A white conjunctiva with watering points to outflow obstruction, not infection
Mucoid reflux on pressure over the lacrimal sac confirms the diagnosis
Around 90 per cent canalise spontaneously within the first year
Photophobia, corneal clouding or enlargement mandate urgent ophthalmology review
A tender red swelling over the sac is dacryocystitis needing systemic antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Massage is most effective when applied as firm downward strokes from the medial canthus along the side of the nose two to three times daily, because the hydrostatic pressure generated in the sac is what ruptures the membrane at the valve of Hasner; sideways wiping of the lashes achieves nothing.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction

subtopic_detail: A small pit in front of the ear found at the newborn check in a baby who passed the hearing screen and has no other anomalies
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3 day old girl before discharge from the postnatal ward. The midwife has noted a tiny pit just in front of the right ear, which the parents had not seen. There is no discharge from it and no surrounding redness.

She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with an uncomplicated pregnancy, and the antenatal morphology scan at 20 weeks reported normal anatomy including the kidneys and urinary tract. She is feeding well and has passed urine and meconium. Examination is otherwise entirely normal, including facial symmetry, palate, neck, limbs and cardiovascular examination. Her automated auditory brainstem response newborn hearing screen was passed in both ears yesterday. There is no family history of deafness or kidney disease.

data_table.Examination: A 1 mm blind ending pit anterior to the right external ear with no discharge or erythema, normally formed and positioned pinnae bilaterally, facial features symmetrical, palate intact, no neck sinuses or branchial remnants, normal cardiovascular and abdominal examination
data_table.Investigations: Automated auditory brainstem response newborn hearing screen passed bilaterally, antenatal morphology scan at 20 weeks reported normal renal tract

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange renal ultrasound to look for structural anomalies
options.rationale: Routine renal imaging for an isolated preauricular pit is no longer recommended, because the yield in an otherwise normal baby with a normal antenatal renal survey is very low. Imaging is indicated when the pit accompanies other dysmorphic features, a branchial sinus, hearing loss or a family history of renal disease or deafness. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal examination)

options.text: Refer for excision of the pit before her first birthday
options.rationale: An asymptomatic pit requires no surgery, and excision is offered only for recurrent infection or discharge from an associated sinus tract. Operating on an uncomplicated pit exposes the infant to anaesthesia and a scar for no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal examination)

options.text: Arrange genetic testing for branchio-oto-renal syndrome
options.rationale: Genetic testing is directed at infants with a syndromic combination such as pits with branchial sinuses, hearing loss and renal anomalies, which is a recognisable phenotype rather than an isolated finding. Here the hearing screen is normal and there are no branchial or renal features to justify it. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Preauricular sinus and pits)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Preauricular sinus and pits

options.text: Repeat the newborn hearing screen at three months of age
options.rationale: A passed automated auditory brainstem response screen does not need repeating on the basis of an isolated ear pit, and scheduling an unnecessary repeat generates parental anxiety. Any later parental or clinician concern about hearing warrants formal audiology assessment regardless of the newborn result. (Source: NSW Health: Statewide Infant Screening Hearing program)
source_refs: NSW Health: Statewide Infant Screening Hearing program

options.text: Reassure, advise on signs of infection, and review as needed
options.rationale: An isolated preauricular pit with a passed hearing screen, no dysmorphic or branchial features and no relevant family history needs no investigation, so explanation with advice to present if the pit becomes red, painful or discharging is the whole management. Ongoing surveillance of hearing and development continues through routine child health checks. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal examination)

explanation.summary: Preauricular pits and sinuses occur in roughly 1 per cent of newborns and arise from incomplete fusion of the hillocks that form the external ear. Older teaching linked any external ear anomaly to renal tract malformation and generated routine renal ultrasound, but the evidence supporting that in an isolated pit with an otherwise normal examination is weak, and current Australian practice reserves imaging for babies with additional features. The syndromic associations worth knowing are branchio-oto-renal syndrome, in which pits accompany branchial sinuses, sensorineural or mixed hearing loss and renal anomalies, and the broader group of babies with several minor anomalies who merit genetic review. The practical risk to the individual child is infection of an associated sinus tract, which can become a recurrent abscess requiring complete excision.
key_points: Isolated pits occur in about 1 per cent of newborns and need no imaging
Additional dysmorphic, branchial, auditory or renal features change the plan
A passed newborn hearing screen does not need repeating for a pit alone
Surgery is for recurrent infection or discharge, not for the pit itself
A pit plus branchial sinus plus hearing loss suggests a syndromic diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Incision and drainage of an infected preauricular sinus leaves the tract behind and recurrence is the rule, so once infection has settled the definitive step is complete excision of the tract, typically after a course of antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus.

sources.label: NSW Health: Statewide Infant Screening Hearing program
BMJ Best Practice: Preauricular sinus and pits

subtopic_detail: A soft bulge at the navel in a one year old that pushes back easily and enlarges when he cries
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 12 month old boy at his immunisation visit. His mother asks about a soft bulge at his navel that has been present since the first weeks of life. It becomes larger when he cries or strains and flattens when he lies quietly. It has never been painful, red or hard, and he has never vomited with it.

He was born at term, is thriving on the 50th centile and is meeting his developmental milestones. On examination there is a 1.5 cm soft swelling at the umbilicus which reduces completely with gentle pressure. The fascial defect admits your fingertip and its edge is smooth and circular. The overlying skin is normal and the abdomen is soft and non-tender.

data_table.Examination: A 1.5 cm soft easily reducible umbilical swelling that enlarges on crying, fascial defect approximately 1 cm admitting a fingertip with a smooth circular edge, overlying skin normal, abdomen soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds, no groin swelling and both testes descended

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Reassure and review, with referral if it persists past age four
options.rationale: Umbilical hernias in children close spontaneously in the great majority of cases as the abdominal wall musculature develops, so observation with review and referral for persistence beyond about 4 to 5 years is standard, and incarceration is rare at this site. Parents are advised to present urgently if the swelling becomes irreducible, painful or discoloured. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Refer for elective repair before he starts kindergarten next year
options.rationale: Repairing at this age operates on a large number of defects that would have closed without surgery, and there is no time pressure because complications are uncommon. Elective repair becomes reasonable once the defect has failed to close by school age or if it is large or symptomatic. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Apply a compressive umbilical band to encourage early closure
options.rationale: Strapping, coins and compression bands do not accelerate fascial closure and can cause skin breakdown under the dressing. They persist as folk remedies but have no place in current management. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Arrange abdominal ultrasound to measure the fascial defect size
options.rationale: The defect is palpable and the diagnosis is clinical, so imaging adds nothing to a decision that rests on age and symptoms. Ultrasound of the abdominal wall is useful where the anatomy is unclear, such as distinguishing an epigastric or paraumbilical hernia from a true umbilical one. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric surgery for repair within four weeks
options.rationale: Urgency is driven by incarceration, which presents with an irreducible tender swelling and vomiting, and none of those features is present in a freely reducible painless hernia. That presentation would require same day surgical assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

explanation.summary: Umbilical hernia in infancy results from incomplete closure of the umbilical ring and is common, particularly in preterm infants and in children of African ancestry. Its natural history contrasts sharply with that of an inguinal hernia in a child: the umbilical defect narrows and closes spontaneously in most children over the first few years, whereas an inguinal hernia does not close and carries a meaningful incarceration risk that mandates early repair. Defect diameter is the most useful predictor of spontaneous closure, with small defects closing readily and defects beyond about 1.5 to 2 cm less likely to do so. Persistent hernias are repaired around school age, both to avoid a cosmetically obvious bulge and because spontaneous closure after that point is unlikely.
key_points: Most paediatric umbilical hernias close spontaneously by 4 to 5 years
Defect diameter predicts closure better than the size of the visible bulge
Incarceration is rare at the umbilicus, unlike in the groin
Compression bands and taping do not aid closure
Irreducibility with pain or vomiting is a same day surgical presentation
explanation.pearls: The contrast worth holding is that an inguinal hernia diagnosed in an infant is referred for repair within weeks because incarceration risk is highest in the first year, while an umbilical hernia of the same size in the same infant is simply reviewed until school age.

sources.label: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons: Paediatric surgery referral guidance

subtopic_detail: An intermittent groin bulge in a three month old born at thirty four weeks with both testes in the scrotum
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 3 month old boy, born at 34 weeks gestation and now 44 weeks corrected. His mother has noticed a bulge in his right groin over the past two weeks. It appears when he cries or strains during a nappy change and disappears when he settles. It has never been tender and he feeds and vomits normally.

He is thriving and had an uncomplicated neonatal course apart from four days of nasal prong oxygen. On examination at rest the groin looks normal. When he cries a smooth swelling appears above and medial to the pubic tubercle, extending towards the scrotum, and it reduces completely with gentle pressure. Both testes are in the scrotum and the right testis is palpable separately from the swelling. There is no erythema and the abdomen is soft.

data_table.Examination: Reducible right inguinal swelling appearing on crying and extending towards the scrotum, reduces fully with gentle pressure, both testes within the scrotum with the right testis palpable separately from the swelling, transillumination not attempted, abdomen soft and non-tender, no erythema or tenderness over the swelling
data_table.Investigations: Weight tracking along the 25th centile on the corrected age chart

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange ultrasound of the groin to confirm the diagnosis first
options.rationale: A reducible swelling appearing on straining above and medial to the pubic tubercle is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging delays a referral whose urgency is driven by age. Ultrasound has a role when the examination is equivocal or when distinguishing a hydrocele of the cord from a hernia is genuinely difficult. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for repair on the next available list
options.rationale: Paediatric inguinal hernias do not resolve spontaneously and the risk of incarceration is highest in the first year of life and higher again in infants born preterm, so prompt referral for herniotomy rather than watchful waiting is correct. Preterm infants also need repair planned with attention to postoperative apnoea monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Advise a reducing truss and review in the surgical clinic later
options.rationale: A truss does not close a patent processus vaginalis and can cause skin breakdown or make a segment of bowel harder to reduce. Mechanical appliances have no place in the management of a paediatric inguinal hernia. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Reassure and review at twelve months, as most close on their own
options.rationale: Spontaneous closure is the natural history of an umbilical hernia, not an inguinal one, where the patent processus vaginalis persists and the bowel remains at risk. Confusing the two natural histories is the central error this presentation tests. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Refer to the emergency department for reduction under sedation now
options.rationale: Emergency reduction is for an incarcerated hernia, which presents as an irreducible tender swelling with a distressed or vomiting infant. This swelling reduces spontaneously and completely, so the pathway is elective rather than emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

explanation.summary: An inguinal hernia in a child is an indirect hernia through a patent processus vaginalis and is far commoner in boys, on the right, and in those born preterm, where the reported incidence reaches 10 to 30 per cent in the most preterm infants. Unlike an umbilical hernia it will not close spontaneously, and the reason for timely surgery is incarceration, which peaks in the first months of life and can compromise bowel or the testicular blood supply. The main differential at this site is a hydrocele of the cord or a communicating hydrocele, which transilluminates, does not extend up to the internal ring on palpation and is not reducible in the same way. In a former preterm infant the anaesthetic plan matters as much as the surgical one, because postoperative apnoea risk persists until around 60 weeks corrected age and mandates postoperative monitoring rather than day surgery.
key_points: A paediatric inguinal hernia will not close spontaneously and needs repair
Incarceration risk is highest in the first year and in preterm infants
Umbilical hernias observe to school age; inguinal hernias are referred promptly
A hydrocele transilluminates and is not reducible in the same way
Former preterm infants need postoperative apnoea monitoring, not day surgery
explanation.pearls: Postoperative apnoea risk after general anaesthesia persists until roughly 60 weeks postconceptional age, so a former 34 week infant repaired at 44 weeks corrected is admitted for overnight cardiorespiratory monitoring rather than discharged the same day.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Perioperative care of the former preterm infant
BMJ Best Practice: Inguinal hernia in children

subtopic_detail: Witnessed pauses in breathing at home in a four week old with three days of coryza but only mild work of breathing in the department
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 4 week old boy, born at 38 weeks, with three days of runny nose and cough. His mother reports he is taking about two thirds of his usual feeds. Twice last night and once this morning she saw him stop breathing for what she estimates was several seconds, going pale and floppy before starting again after she picked him up and rubbed his back.

In the department he is alert and settles in his mother's arms. He has mild subcostal recession with no nasal flaring or head bobbing, and you hear widespread fine crackles on auscultation. His nose is blocked with clear secretions. He has had no fever at home and his nappies remain wet. His vital signs are pulse 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 72/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air and temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Examination: Alert and consolable, mild subcostal recession without nasal flaring or head bobbing, widespread fine inspiratory crackles with no focal consolidation, blocked nose with clear secretions, anterior fontanelle normal, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab sent for respiratory viral panel, no chest radiograph performed, no blood tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Discharge home with feeding advice and general practitioner review
options.rationale: Witnessed apnoea in an infant of this age is an independent indication for admission regardless of how well the child looks at the time of assessment, because apnoea recurs and is not predicted by the degree of respiratory distress. Discharge with review would be reasonable for a well feeding infant with mild bronchiolitis and no apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for a trial of high flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy now
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants who fail low flow oxygen, and this infant is not hypoxaemic at all with an SpO2 of 96 per cent in air, so there is no oxygen requirement to escalate. Admission is right but the intervention attached to it is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and observation
options.rationale: Apnoea is a recognised presentation of bronchiolitis in infants under about 6 to 8 weeks and carries a risk of recurrence, so admission with continuous cardiorespiratory and saturation monitoring plus support of feeding is the appropriate response even when respiratory distress is mild. Treatment otherwise remains supportive, with oxygen only if saturations fall below the accepted threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for nebulised salbutamol and reassessment after two hours
options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not alter the course of bronchiolitis in infants and are not recommended at any severity, because the obstruction is from mucosal oedema and debris rather than reversible smooth muscle constriction. A trial of salbutamol belongs to the assessment of an older wheezing child in whom asthma is plausible. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Observe for two hours in the department and then discharge home
options.rationale: A short observation period is not sufficient to exclude recurrent apnoea, which is characteristically intermittent and often occurs overnight during sleep. Brief departmental observation is appropriate for assessing feeding in a well older infant, not for clearing apnoea in a neonate. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the commonest reason for infant admission in Australia and is managed supportively with attention to feeding and oxygenation, since bronchodilators, corticosteroids, adrenaline and antibiotics have no routine role. Severity assessment is based on work of breathing, feeding, oxygen saturation and apnoea, and the last of these behaves differently from the others because it can occur in an infant whose respiratory examination looks unremarkable. Young age is the dominant risk factor, with apnoea concentrated in infants under 6 to 8 weeks and in those born preterm, and it is one of the few features in bronchiolitis that mandates admission on its own. Where oxygen is needed, Australian practice starts with low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L per minute and reserves high flow for failure of low flow.
key_points: Witnessed apnoea mandates admission irrespective of work of breathing
Apnoea risk concentrates in infants under 6 to 8 weeks and in preterm infants
Management is supportive; bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended
Low flow nasal prong oxygen is first line if oxygen is required
Feeding adequacy and hydration drive the other admission decisions
explanation.pearls: The RCH oxygen threshold in bronchiolitis is a saturation below 90 per cent rather than the 92 to 94 per cent many candidates quote, so an infant sitting at 91 per cent with mild recession and adequate feeding does not need oxygen, while this infant needs admission for apnoea despite a saturation of 96 per cent.

subtopic_detail: A thriving three week old referred after newborn screening showed a raised trypsinogen with two variants found on the screening gene panel
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a respiratory clinic seeing a 3 week old girl referred after newborn bloodspot screening. The laboratory reported an immunoreactive trypsinogen level above the screening cut off, and the reflex gene panel identified two variants in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene, one of which the laboratory has classified as being of uncertain clinical significance.

The parents are distressed and want to know whether their daughter has cystic fibrosis. She was born at term, passed meconium on day one and is breastfeeding well. Her weight has risen from 3.2 kg at birth to 3.6 kg today, tracking along the 50th centile. Examination is normal with a clear chest, no clubbing and a soft abdomen. Her stools are described by her mother as soft and yellow without any oily appearance.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and alert, chest clear on auscultation with no recession, abdomen soft with no organomegaly, no digital clubbing, hydration normal
data_table.Investigations: Newborn bloodspot immunoreactive trypsinogen above the screening cut off, reflex cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator panel reporting two variants with one classified as of uncertain significance, weight 3.6 kg tracking on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Start pancreatic enzyme replacement and airway clearance now
options.rationale: Treatment should not begin before the diagnosis is established, and this baby has normal growth and no features of fat malabsorption to justify enzyme replacement. Enzymes are started once pancreatic insufficiency is demonstrated, guided by faecal elastase and growth. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.text: Repeat the immunoreactive trypsinogen level in four weeks time
options.rationale: Trypsinogen falls with age irrespective of whether the infant has cystic fibrosis, so a repeat level is uninterpretable and cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Its only role is as the first tier of the screening algorithm on the newborn bloodspot. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.text: Arrange faecal elastase measurement to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Faecal elastase measures exocrine pancreatic function and guides enzyme replacement, but it neither confirms nor excludes cystic fibrosis because a proportion of affected children are pancreatic sufficient at diagnosis. It is a functional test rather than a diagnostic one. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.text: Arrange sweat chloride testing at an accredited paediatric centre
options.rationale: Sweat chloride measurement remains the diagnostic test that resolves a positive screen, and it is essential here because one variant is of uncertain significance so the genotype cannot establish the diagnosis on its own. Testing is performed at an accredited centre once the infant is over 2 kg and at least 2 weeks old, with a chloride of 60 mmol/L or more diagnostic. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

options.text: Reassure the parents, as the baby is thriving and asymptomatic
options.rationale: Normal growth at 3 weeks does not exclude the diagnosis, since the majority of infants identified by screening are asymptomatic at that age and the point of screening is to intervene before deterioration. Reassurance without completing the diagnostic pathway risks a late diagnosis after preventable lung injury. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Nationally agreed newborn screening pathway

explanation.summary: Australian newborn bloodspot screening for cystic fibrosis uses immunoreactive trypsinogen as a first tier, then a gene panel on trypsinogen positive samples, and refers those with one or two variants for definitive testing. Genotype alone is often insufficient because panels include variants of uncertain significance and variants with variable clinical consequence, so sweat chloride remains the arbiter, with values of 60 mmol/L or more diagnostic, 30 to 59 mmol/L intermediate and requiring extended genotyping and follow up, and under 30 mmol/L making the diagnosis unlikely. Infants with an intermediate result and inconclusive genotyping are labelled as having a screen positive inconclusive diagnosis and enter structured surveillance rather than treatment. Prompt resolution matters because early nutritional support and airway surveillance in a specialist centre are what convert a screening programme into improved long term lung function.
key_points: Trypsinogen screens, genotype triages, sweat chloride diagnoses
A variant of uncertain significance prevents diagnosis on genotype alone
Sweat chloride 60 mmol/L or more is diagnostic; under 30 mmol/L makes it unlikely
Faecal elastase guides enzyme replacement but does not diagnose the condition
Normal growth at a few weeks of age does not exclude the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Sweat testing requires an adequate sweat weight, so it is scheduled once the infant is at least 2 weeks old and over 2 kg; an inadequate collection is reported as a failed test and must be repeated rather than read as a low chloride.

subtopic_detail: A six week old needing tube feeds for a weak suck with marked floppiness through the trunk but brisk knee reflexes and undescended testes
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 week old boy who has needed nasogastric top up feeds since birth because he tires after a few sucks and milk spills from his mouth. His mother recalls that he moved much less in the womb than her older child did.

He was born at 39 weeks in good condition. On examination he is alert and makes eye contact, but he slips through your hands on vertical suspension and drapes over your forearm on ventral suspension. His cry is weak. His deep tendon reflexes are present and brisk at the knees and ankles, his tongue shows no fasciculation and there is no ptosis or facial weakness. Both testes are impalpable and the scrotum is underdeveloped. His creatine kinase is 96 U/L (less than 200).

data_table.Examination: Alert with normal social response, marked axial hypotonia with head lag and draping on ventral suspension, weak cry, limb power reduced but antigravity movement present, deep tendon reflexes present and brisk at knees and ankles, no tongue fasciculation, no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia, both testes impalpable with a hypoplastic scrotum
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 96 U/L (less than 200), sodium 139 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), thyroid stimulating hormone and free thyroxine within normal limits, cranial ultrasound reported as normal

lead_in: Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: SMN1 gene deletion testing for spinal muscular atrophy
options.rationale: Anterior horn cell disease produces absent rather than brisk deep tendon reflexes, usually with tongue fasciculation and paradoxical breathing, and it does not cause cryptorchidism. Preserved brisk reflexes are the finding that makes this diagnosis unlikely and points away from a lower motor neuron cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

options.text: Muscle biopsy to look for a congenital myopathy or dystrophy
options.rationale: A normal creatine kinase and preserved reflexes make a primary muscle disorder much less likely, and biopsy is an invasive test to select after non-invasive genetic testing has been exhausted. Congenital myotonic dystrophy would also be expected to produce facial weakness and a history of maternal symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

options.text: Repeat creatine kinase with nerve conduction and electromyography
options.rationale: Neurophysiology localises weakness to nerve, junction or muscle, and here the clinical pattern of central hypotonia with preserved reflexes already points above the motor unit. These studies are uncomfortable in a neonate and are reserved for suspected peripheral causes. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

options.text: Maternal and infant acetylcholine receptor antibody measurement
options.rationale: Transient neonatal myasthenia from transplacental antibody presents with ptosis, poor suck and fatigable weakness in the infant of a mother with myasthenia, and it resolves over weeks. There is no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia here and no maternal history. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

options.text: DNA methylation analysis of the chromosome 15 imprinted region
options.rationale: Severe central hypotonia with a weak suck requiring tube feeding, reduced foetal movements, cryptorchidism and preserved reflexes with a normal creatine kinase is the neonatal phenotype of a disorder of imprinting at chromosome 15, and methylation analysis detects all molecular subtypes including deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects. Standard karyotype and microarray can miss uniparental disomy, which is why methylation testing is the specific first line test. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant)

explanation.summary: The first task in assessing a floppy infant is to separate central from peripheral hypotonia, because that distinction redirects the entire investigation pathway. Central causes preserve or exaggerate deep tendon reflexes and are often accompanied by reduced alertness, seizures or dysmorphic features, whereas peripheral causes at the anterior horn cell, nerve, junction or muscle typically depress or abolish reflexes and may raise creatine kinase. Prader-Willi syndrome is a leading genetic cause of profound neonatal central hypotonia and is recognised by the combination of severe feeding difficulty needing tube feeds, reduced antenatal movement, hypogonadism and later hyperphagia with developmental delay. Early diagnosis changes management substantially, since growth hormone therapy, dietetic and feeding support and structured monitoring for obesity, scoliosis and sleep disordered breathing all begin in infancy.
key_points: Preserved or brisk reflexes point to a central rather than peripheral cause
Normal creatine kinase argues against a primary muscle disorder
Tube feeding for a weak suck plus cryptorchidism is a recognisable phenotype
Methylation analysis detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects
Microarray alone can miss uniparental disomy and is not sufficient
explanation.pearls: The feeding pattern inverts over early childhood in this condition, with profound infantile feeding failure giving way to hyperphagia from around 2 years, so the infant who needed nasogastric feeds becomes the child who needs supervised food access and early growth hormone referral.

subtopic_detail: Breast tissue in a fourteen year old boy whose height is above the ninety seventh centile with small firm testes and difficulty at school
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 14 year old boy brought by his father because of breast tissue that has been present for about a year and is causing him distress in the school change rooms. He is otherwise well and takes no medication or supplements.

His father mentions in passing that he has always needed extra help with reading and written work and has recently been assessed for learning support. On examination there is 3 cm of firm glandular tissue beneath each areola. His height is above the 97th centile while his father and mother are both of average height, and his arm span exceeds his height with relatively long legs. Pubic hair is Tanner stage 4. Both testes are descended but measure approximately 3 mL each and feel firm, with no palpable mass in either testis.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral firm glandular breast tissue 3 cm beneath each areola without discharge, height above the 97th centile with arm span exceeding height and relatively long lower limbs, pubic hair Tanner stage 4, both testes descended measuring approximately 3 mL and firm in consistency with no palpable mass, no hepatomegaly, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and free thyroxine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his assessment?

options.text: Measure gonadotrophins and testosterone, and request a karyotype
options.rationale: Small firm testes of 3 mL despite Tanner 4 pubic hair, tall stature disproportionate to parental heights with long limbs, and a history of learning difficulty together point to primary testicular failure from a sex chromosome aneuploidy, and the biochemical pattern of raised gonadotrophins with low or low normal testosterone alongside a karyotype establishes it. Pubertal gynaecomastia is excluded by the testicular findings rather than by the breast tissue itself. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Reassure him that this will resolve within about eighteen months
options.rationale: Reassurance is the correct management of physiological pubertal gynaecomastia, which occurs at mid puberty in a boy whose testes are enlarging normally to 12 mL or more and who is growing along his expected centile. Small firm testes with disproportionate tall stature is the pattern that makes that reassurance unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Request testicular ultrasound to exclude an oestrogen secreting tumour
options.rationale: A hormone secreting testicular tumour typically produces asymmetric testicular enlargement or a palpable mass, and both testes here are small, symmetrical and free of any mass. Ultrasound earns its place when a testis is asymmetrically enlarged or a nodule is felt. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Repeat thyroid and liver function testing with a prolactin level
options.rationale: Thyrotoxicosis, chronic liver disease and hyperprolactinaemia all cause gynaecomastia, but thyroid and liver function are already documented as normal and prolactin excess would be expected to suppress rather than preserve pubertal virilisation. Repeating normal tests does not address the testicular finding that drives this presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Refer for surgical reduction of the breast tissue later this year
options.rationale: Surgery addresses the symptom while leaving an unrecognised cause of hypogonadism untreated, and it is considered only for persistent gynaecomastia after the underlying cause has been established and treated. Proceeding to surgery first also forfeits the chance to start testosterone at the right developmental point. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Gynaecomastia is present in up to two thirds of boys at mid puberty and reflects a transient imbalance between oestrogen and androgen action, resolving within 18 to 24 months in the great majority. The clinical task is to identify the minority in whom it signals pathology, and the most useful discriminator is testicular volume, because physiological gynaecomastia occurs in a boy whose testes are enlarging normally. Small firm testes with advanced pubic hair indicate that adrenal androgens are driving virilisation while the testes are failing, and in a tall boy with long limbs and educational difficulty this is the classic presentation of Klinefelter syndrome, which affects roughly 1 in 600 males and is substantially underdiagnosed. Diagnosis matters because testosterone replacement supports virilisation, bone density and wellbeing, and because fertility preservation options are best discussed in adolescence.
key_points: Testicular volume, not breast size, separates physiological from pathological gynaecomastia
Small firm testes with Tanner 4 pubic hair indicate primary testicular failure
Raised gonadotrophins with low testosterone confirm a primary gonadal problem
Tall stature with long limbs and learning difficulty supports sex chromosome aneuploidy
Drugs, thyrotoxicosis, liver disease and testicular tumours are the other causes to exclude
explanation.pearls: Testicular volume above about 12 mL at Tanner 4 fits physiological pubertal gynaecomastia, whereas volumes under about 6 mL at the same pubic hair stage should trigger gonadotrophin measurement and a karyotype, since Klinefelter syndrome is diagnosed in only about a quarter of affected males across their lifetime.

subtopic_detail: Tummy aches and loose motions with weight crossing centiles in a nine year old whose parents removed all wheat six weeks before the blood test was taken
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 9 year old girl referred with eight months of intermittent tummy aches and loose motions two or three times a day. Her weight has fallen from the 50th to the 15th centile over that period while her height has stayed on the 40th centile.

Six weeks before the blood test was taken, her parents removed all bread, pasta and cereal from her diet after reading about wheat intolerance, and they report her tummy aches are now much less frequent. Her general practitioner then arranged blood tests. Examination shows a slim girl with no abdominal distension, no mouth ulcers and no perianal abnormality; her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her parents are willing to follow whatever plan you recommend but are reluctant to make her unwell again without good reason.

data_table.Examination: Slim build with weight on the 15th centile and height on the 40th centile, abdomen soft and non-tender with no distension or mass, no mouth ulcers, no clubbing, no perianal skin tags or fissures, Tanner stage 1
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase IgA negative, total IgA within normal limits, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 155), mean cell volume 79 fL (77 to 95), ferritin 14 micrograms/L (15 to 200), C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), faecal calprotectin within normal limits, HLA DQ2 positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Accept the negative serology and investigate other causes of her symptoms
options.rationale: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies fall once gluten is withdrawn, so a negative result taken after six weeks of exclusion cannot be interpreted as evidence against the diagnosis. Treating this serology as a true negative is the specific trap in a child already on a restricted diet. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Reintroduce gluten daily for at least six weeks, then repeat the testing
options.rationale: Valid serology and histology both require adequate gluten intake, so a formal gluten challenge of the equivalent of around four slices of bread daily for six weeks or more must precede repeat antibody testing and any biopsy, and her falling centiles with iron deficiency make completing the diagnosis important rather than optional. The positive HLA result is used only to show the diagnosis remains possible, since it is common in the general population. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Refer for duodenal biopsy now while she continues to avoid all gluten
options.rationale: Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet, so a biopsy taken now may be normal in a child who genuinely has the condition and would leave her wrongly labelled for life. Biopsy is the right test but only after an adequate gluten challenge has restored the antigenic stimulus. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Diagnose coeliac disease on the basis of the positive HLA DQ2 result
options.rationale: Around half of the Australian population carries a permissive HLA type, so a positive result has almost no positive predictive value and cannot diagnose the condition. Its value is the reverse: absence of both permissive haplotypes makes the diagnosis very unlikely and can spare a child a gluten challenge. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Repeat the tissue transglutaminase level in three months without changing her diet
options.rationale: Repeating the antibody on an unchanged gluten free diet will simply reproduce a negative result, because the antibody titre reflects current gluten exposure rather than underlying susceptibility. A repeat level is informative only once gluten has been reintroduced. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

explanation.summary: Coeliac disease requires gluten exposure to be diagnosed, because both the serological and histological abnormalities are consequences of an active immune response to dietary gluten and both normalise on exclusion. This makes a family initiated gluten free diet one of the commonest reasons a child ends up with an unresolvable diagnostic question, and the only way out is a formal gluten challenge with repeat serology and, in most children, duodenal biopsy. HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing is frequently misused in this situation: the haplotypes are carried by a large minority of the population so a positive result is not diagnostic, but their absence has a high negative predictive value and can end the investigation. The reason to persist rather than accept an empirical gluten free diet is that a confirmed diagnosis brings coeliac specific follow up, screening of first degree relatives, bone and nutritional surveillance and access to dietetic support, while an unconfirmed label commits a child to lifelong restriction without any of that.
key_points: Serology and histology both normalise on a gluten free diet
A gluten challenge must precede repeat serology or biopsy
HLA DQ2 or DQ8 positivity is common and not diagnostic; absence largely excludes
Falling centiles with iron deficiency makes completing the diagnosis important
An unconfirmed label forfeits coeliac specific follow up and family screening
explanation.pearls: An adequate paediatric gluten challenge is the equivalent of about four slices of wheat bread daily for a minimum of six weeks before retesting, and if a child cannot tolerate that, HLA typing is the test to request first because a negative result removes the need for the challenge altogether.

sources.label: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease
